passage:
Note from Disha's class teacher.
During the colour card game, Devika saw Disha hide a red card under her knee. "You cheated!" she said. The other children stared. Disha's face went bright red and she ran to the cubby corner and hid behind the coats. I went and sat outside the cubby. I did not call her bad. I said, "Everyone makes mistakes in games. Shall we say sorry and play again, fair this time?" After a while she came out. She told Devika, "Sorry." They played two more rounds, and Disha kept all her cards on the mat.

qa.q: Where did Disha hide the red card?
qa.a: She hid it under her knee.

qa.q: What does Disha running to the cubby suggest she felt?
qa.a: She felt deeply ashamed and embarrassed at being caught, and wanted to run away and hide.

qa.q: How did the teacher help without making the shame worse?
qa.a: The teacher sat nearby, did not call her bad, and offered a way to say sorry and play again fairly.

qa.q: How might Devika feel when Disha says sorry?
qa.a: Devika may feel the game is fair again and be glad to keep playing with Disha.

grounding: A young girl caught cheating feels hot-faced shame and wants to run, and a teacher helps her say sorry and try again fairly.

passage: The children were playing lagori behind the temple, stacking seven flat stones. Ishita stepped over the line to throw from closer. "Ishita cheated!" Irawati shouted. Everyone turned. Ishita's face went hot. She dropped the ball and began to run towards home. An older cousin yelled, "Cheater girl! Bad girl!" Ishita ran faster. Dadi, sitting on the temple steps, called her back gently. "Come, sit." Ishita sat, head down. "You made a mistake. You're not bad. Say sorry, and try from behind the line." Ishita whispered sorry to Irawati. Her next throw knocked down three stones.

qa.q: How many flat stones were stacked for lagori?
qa.a: Seven flat stones were stacked.

qa.q: How was Ishita feeling as she ran towards home?
qa.a: She felt ashamed and hot-faced at being caught, and wanted to run away, especially after being called a bad girl.

qa.q: What made Dadi's response wiser than the cousin's?
qa.a: Dadi separated the mistake from Ishita, saying she was not bad, and helped her say sorry and play again fairly; the cousin's label only made her run.

qa.q: How might Irawati see Ishita's whispered sorry?
qa.a: She may feel it's fair again and be happy to keep playing, seeing Ishita really throw from behind the line. 🙂

grounding: A young girl caught cheating feels ashamed and runs, and her grandmother helps her say sorry and try again fairly rather than calling her bad.

passage: In the clinic waiting room, Mummy was filling in a form. Karthik drew noughts and crosses on a paper. "New rule," he said. "I get two turns. And if I say 'diagonal' I win." Neelam's crosses kept losing. "New rule: crosses can't go in corners." Neelam's cheeks burned. She felt small and stuck. Karthik always won. She stood up. "That is not fair!" Then she tugged Mummy's sleeve. "Karthik keeps making rules so he wins." Mummy looked at the paper. "Karthik, same rules for both. And sometimes letting your little sister win is kind." Karthik sighed and drew a new grid.

qa.q: What was Mummy doing in the waiting room?
qa.a: Mummy was filling in a form.

qa.q: How did Neelam feel as Karthik kept adding rules?
qa.a: She felt angry and powerless, small and stuck because he always won.

qa.q: What did Neelam do that was wise?
qa.a: She said "That is not fair!" and asked Mummy for help instead of giving up or hitting.

qa.q: How might Karthik see Mummy's new rule?
qa.a: He may feel annoyed at first, but it could teach him that fair play and letting his sister win sometimes is kind.

grounding: A young girl's older brother keeps inventing rules to win, and she says it's not fair and asks a parent for help.

passage:
Monday: Nilesh and Tanvir played cars. Nilesh said, "My car wins because it's red." Tanvir's car was blue. He threw it down and cried, feeling there was nothing he could do.
Wednesday: "My car wins because it's bigger." Tanvir scowled. Then he said loudly, "That is not fair!" He went to find Papa. Papa sat with them. "Same rules for both. Whoever reaches the door first wins."
Saturday: The cars raced to the door. Tanvir's blue car won. Nilesh groaned, then laughed. "Okay, little one. You won fair and square."

qa.q: Why did Nilesh say his car won on Monday?
qa.a: He said his car won because it was red.

qa.q: How did Tanvir feel on Monday when he threw his car down?
qa.a: He felt angry and powerless, as if there was nothing he could do against his older brother's rules.

qa.q: What changed on Wednesday?
qa.a: Tanvir said "That is not fair!" and asked Papa, who set one rule for both boys.

qa.q: How might Nilesh feel when Tanvir wins fair and square?
qa.a: He may feel a little disappointed but also kind and big-brotherly, since he laughs and praises Tanvir.

grounding: Over a week, a younger boy whose older brother makes up winning rules speaks up and gets a parent's help to play fair.

passage: Ayesha Mami had come from Lucknow to the village for Saurabh's birthday. She handed him a box wrapped in newspaper and string. Saurabh tore it open. Socks. Brown woolly socks. His face dropped. He had hoped for a toy tractor. Amma gave him a tiny nudge. Saurabh swallowed. "Thank you, Mami." Mami smiled. "For the cold mornings, when you walk to school." That night, Saurabh cried a little into Amma's lap. "I wanted a tractor." Amma stroked his hair. "Mami knitted those herself, for your feet. That's her love in wool."

qa.q: What was the box wrapped in?
qa.a: It was wrapped in newspaper and string.

qa.q: How did Saurabh feel when he saw the socks?
qa.a: He felt disappointed and sad, because he had hoped for a toy tractor, and his face dropped.

qa.q: What did Saurabh do well at the moment of opening the gift?
qa.a: He said thank you first and waited to cry about it later at home with Amma.

qa.q: How might Ayesha Mami feel if Saurabh wears the socks on a cold morning?
qa.a: She would likely feel happy and loved back, since she knitted them herself for him.

grounding: A young boy is disappointed to get socks instead of a toy, says thank you first and cries later, and learns the gift carries love.

passage: The parcel from Grandpa arrived in Toronto on a snowy afternoon. Tariq ripped the paper. Inside were socks, with little whales on them. No toy. Tariq's face crumpled. His mother, Soo-ah, held up the phone. Grandpa was on video, waving. "Do you like them?" Tariq looked at Mom. He took a shaky breath. "Thank you, Grandpa." After the call, he buried his face in a cushion. "I wanted a robot." Soo-ah sat beside him. "It's okay to feel disappointed. Grandpa picked whales because you told him you love them." Tariq peeked at the socks.

qa.q: What was on the socks?
qa.a: The socks had little whales on them.

qa.q: How was Tariq feeling when his face crumpled?
qa.a: He felt disappointed and sad that the parcel held socks and no toy.

qa.q: What did Soo-ah teach Tariq after the call?
qa.a: She said it was okay to feel disappointed and showed him the gift was chosen with love, because Grandpa remembered he loves whales.

qa.q: How might Grandpa see Tariq's thank you on the video call?
qa.a: He likely feels happy and warm, glad his grandson liked the socks he picked. 😊

grounding: A young boy is disappointed by socks from his grandfather, thanks him first, and later learns the gift was a sign of love.

passage: At the birthday party in their Chennai flat, Saurabh Mama gave Ganga a big box. She opened it in front of everyone. A book about birds. Ganga looked at it and said loudly, "I don't like this. I wanted slime." The room went quiet. Mama's smile wobbled. Amma knelt beside Ganga. "Can you say, 'Thank you, Mama, it was kind of you'?" Ganga said it slowly. Later, when the guests had gone, Amma asked, "What did you really feel?" "Sad," Ganga said. "I really wanted slime." Amma nodded. "Thank you for telling me now."

qa.q: What did Ganga want instead of the book?
qa.a: She wanted slime.

qa.q: Why did Ganga say "I don't like this" out loud?
qa.a: She was not trying to be rude; she felt disappointed and simply said what she felt, as young children do.

qa.q: How did Amma handle Ganga's words wisely?
qa.a: She showed Ganga a kind thank-you to say to Mama, then later listened to her real feelings in private.

qa.q: What is it like for Saurabh Mama when Ganga says she doesn't like it?
qa.a: His smile wobbles, so he likely feels hurt and a bit embarrassed in front of everyone.

grounding: A young girl says she doesn't like a gift in front of the giver, and her mother models a kind thank-you and later hears her real feelings.

passage:
"Look, Akash! Nana sent you a kurta for Diwali."
Akash held it up. "I don't like this. It's itchy and yellow."
"Akash..." Bhavna glanced at Nana on the video call.
Nana laughed, but softly.
"Beta, you can say, 'Thank you, Nana, it was kind of you.'"
"Thank you, Nana. It was kind of you."
"You're welcome, my boy!"
After the call, Bhavna sat with him. "Now tell me really."
"It is itchy, Mumma. I wasn't being mean."
"I know. We'll wear a soft vest under it."

qa.q: What did Nana send Akash?
qa.a: Nana sent him a kurta for Diwali.

qa.q: How did Akash feel when he said he didn't like the kurta?
qa.a: He felt disappointed and uncomfortable because it was itchy; he wasn't trying to be mean, just saying what he felt.

qa.q: What did Bhavna do that a wise parent would do?
qa.a: She showed him a kind way to thank Nana, then listened to his real feeling afterwards and found a fix.

qa.q: How might Nana feel when Akash says it's itchy and yellow?
qa.a: Nana may feel a small sting, but laughs softly, understanding that small children say what they feel.

grounding: A young boy says he doesn't like a gift in front of the giver, and his mother shows him a kind thank-you and later hears his real feelings.

passage: Imran Chacha had searched three shops in the old city for the doll with the blue frock. At Kashish's birthday in the crowded flat, he handed it over. Kashish unwrapped it and wrinkled her nose. "Eww. Dolls are for babies." Imran felt a little drop in his chest. He had hoped to see her smile. Kashish's mother started to scold. Imran touched her arm. "It's okay. She's five. They don't hide things." He crouched down. "Well, I tried! But you know, a thank-you makes the giver happy." Kashish thought, then mumbled, "Thank you, Chacha."

qa.q: How many shops did Imran Chacha search?
qa.a: He searched three shops in the old city.

qa.q: How did Imran feel when Kashish wrinkled her nose?
qa.a: He felt sad and a little hurt, a drop in his chest, because he had hoped she would smile.

qa.q: Why did Imran stop Kashish's mother from scolding?
qa.a: He understood small children don't hide feelings, so he chose to keep it light and gently remind her that thanks matter.

qa.q: How might Kashish feel after Chacha's gentle words?
qa.a: She may feel a bit sheepish but not ashamed, and ready to say thank you.

grounding: An uncle feels hurt when a small child makes a face at his gift, but he doesn't scold, keeps it light and reminds her thanks matter.

passage:
"Rafiq, happy birthday! This is from Keerthana Athai."
Rafiq opened the packet. A box of coloured pencils. He pulled a face. "Pencils? I have pencils."
Keerthana felt a small ache. She had chosen the forty-eight colours box.
"Rafiq!" his father said sharply.
"Leave it," said Keerthana. "Little ones say what they see." She smiled at Rafiq. "Well, these have gold and silver in them. And you know what? When someone gives you something, a thank-you makes them feel good."
Rafiq looked in the box. "Gold? ...Thank you, Athai."

qa.q: How many colours were in the pencil box?
qa.a: It was the forty-eight colours box.

qa.q: How did Keerthana feel when Rafiq pulled a face?
qa.a: She felt a small ache of sadness and hurt, because she had chosen the gift carefully.

qa.q: What did Keerthana do instead of scolding?
qa.a: She kept it light, showed him the gold and silver pencils, and reminded him that a thank-you makes the giver feel good.

qa.q: How might Rafiq's father see Keerthana's response?
qa.a: He may feel relieved and grateful that she was not offended and helped Rafiq learn kindly.

grounding: An aunt feels hurt when a small child makes a face at her gift, but she stays light and reminds him that thanks matter.

passage: In a flat in Copenhagen, Emil knelt at the table with his tongue poking out. He drew a big green dinosaur, a birthday cake with five candles and Kwame's name in wobbly letters. He added glitter. Lots of glitter. The next morning at kindergarten he ran to Kwame, holding the card behind his back. "Surprise!" Emil's smile was so big his cheeks hurt. Kwame opened it. "A dinosaur! For me?" "I made it myself," Emil said, bouncing. "The glitter took ages." Kwame held it up to show everyone.

qa.q: How many candles were on the cake Emil drew?
qa.a: He drew a birthday cake with five candles.

qa.q: What was Emil feeling when he ran to Kwame with the card?
qa.a: He felt excited and loving, so happy that his cheeks hurt from smiling, and eager for Kwame to like it.

qa.q: What does Emil's card show about giving?
qa.a: It shows that love is in the effort, since he made it himself and spent ages on the glitter.

qa.q: How might Kwame feel when he holds the card up?
qa.a: Kwame probably feels special and proud that a friend made a card just for this birthday. 🎉

grounding: A young boy makes a birthday card for his friend and gives it with a big smile, excited that his friend will like it.

passage: At the daycare craft table, Reena folded a pink paper into a card. "It's for Payal. It's her birthday." She drew Payal with a crown and herself holding a balloon. The helper aunty spelled "Happy Birthday" for her, and Reena copied it slowly. At home time, she ran to Payal in the line, card held high. "I made it! Just for you!" Reena was hopping. Payal looked and giggled. "I have a crown!" Reena beamed. "Because it's your birthday, you're the queen."

qa.q: What colour paper did Reena use?
qa.a: She folded a pink paper into a card.

qa.q: How can you tell Reena was excited to give the card?
qa.a: She ran to Payal with the card held high and was hopping as she gave it.

qa.q: Why might a handmade card mean more than a bought one?
qa.a: It shows the effort and thought Reena put in, like drawing Payal with a crown and copying the words slowly.

qa.q: What is it like for Payal to get this card?
qa.a: She feels delighted and special, giggling at the crown her friend drew for her.

grounding: A young girl makes a birthday card for her friend and gives it excitedly, showing love through effort.

passage:
"Lakshmi, close your eyes!"
"Why, Nirmala?"
"Just close them! Now open!"
Nirmala held out a drawing: two girls holding hands under a big yellow sun, with "LAKSHMI" written in orange.
Lakshmi gasped. "That's us!"
"I did it at home. Do you like it?"
Lakshmi hugged the paper to her chest. "Thank you, I love it!" Then she hugged Nirmala too, paper and all.
"Careful, it'll crumple!"
"Tomorrow I'll draw one for you. With a rainbow."
Nirmala grinned. "Two rainbows."

qa.q: What colour was Lakshmi's name written in?
qa.a: It was written in orange.

qa.q: How did Lakshmi feel when she saw the drawing?
qa.a: She felt loved and delighted, gasping and hugging the paper to her chest.

qa.q: What did Lakshmi do that shows gratitude well?
qa.a: She said a warm "Thank you, I love it," hugged her friend and planned to draw one back.

qa.q: How might Nirmala feel when Lakshmi hugs the drawing?
qa.a: Nirmala probably feels happy and proud that her gift was loved.

grounding: A young girl receives a drawing from her friend, thanks her warmly and wants to give one back.

passage:
Note from Hafsa's class teacher, for home.
Today Tanuja gave Hafsa a drawing of a cat in a party hat. Hafsa held it up and said, "Thank you, I love it!" and hugged it against her tummy. She smiled all through lunch and kept peeping at it inside her bag. At colouring time, she asked me for a fresh paper. "I want to make one for Tanuja," she said. She drew a cat too, "so they can be friends." Please look at her drawing tonight; it matters to her. 🙂

qa.q: What did Tanuja draw for Hafsa?
qa.a: Tanuja drew a cat in a party hat.

qa.q: How did Hafsa feel about the drawing?
qa.a: She felt loved and happy, smiling through lunch and peeping at it in her bag.

qa.q: What could Hafsa's family do tonight to encourage her?
qa.a: They could look at the drawing and praise her kind thank-you and her idea of drawing one back for Tanuja.

qa.q: How might Tanuja feel when she gets Hafsa's cat drawing?
qa.a: Tanuja may feel delighted and closer to Hafsa, seeing her gift come back as another gift.

grounding: A young girl thanks her friend warmly for a drawing and wants to give one back, showing how gifts warm friendships.

passage: In Buenos Aires, Yosef spent all Saturday morning on the card. He drew Papa fixing the bicycle, with a spanner as big as his arm. His sister, Rosa, helped him fold it. When Papa came home from work, Yosef ran to the door. "For you!" Papa opened it slowly and studied every line. "Is this me with the bike?" Yosef nodded hard. Papa walked to the fridge, moved the shopping list, and pressed the card up with two magnets. "Right in the middle," he said. Yosef stood beside the fridge, chest puffed out, and looked at it for a long time.

qa.q: Who helped Yosef fold the card?
qa.a: His sister, Rosa, helped him fold it.

qa.q: How did Yosef feel standing beside the fridge?
qa.a: He felt proud, with his chest puffed out, because Papa had put his card right in the middle.

qa.q: Why does Papa's choice to put the card on the fridge matter?
qa.a: It showed Yosef that his gift and effort were valued, not just accepted politely.

qa.q: How might Papa feel studying every line of the card?
qa.a: He likely feels touched and loved, noticing the care his son put into the drawing.

grounding: A young boy gives his father a handmade card, and his father treasures it on the fridge, making the boy feel proud.

passage: Nitin's papa, Lokesh, worked in the hospital canteen. On Saturday Nitin came along with Amma and gave him a folded card. On it was a crayon drawing of Papa with a big pot and a chef's hat. "I made it," Nitin said, suddenly shy. Lokesh wiped his hands on his apron and held it carefully. Then he walked to the big steel fridge behind the counter and stuck it there with tape. "Now everyone who comes for tea will see what my son made." Nitin looked at the fridge, then at the nurses queuing for tea, and grinned from ear to ear.

qa.q: Where did Lokesh work?
qa.a: He worked in the hospital canteen.

qa.q: What was Nitin feeling when he grinned from ear to ear?
qa.a: He felt proud and happy that Papa had put his card where everyone could see it.

qa.q: What did Lokesh do that teaches Nitin his effort matters?
qa.a: He held the card carefully, stuck it on the canteen fridge and said everyone would see what his son made.

qa.q: How might the nurses queuing for tea see the card?
qa.a: They might smile and feel warmed by it, seeing a child's love for his father on the fridge.

grounding: A young boy gives his father a handmade card, and his father proudly puts it on the fridge at work, making him feel proud.

passage: In the clinic waiting room, Usha lay across Mummy's lap, her cheeks hot and red. Everything felt heavy, even her eyelids. Mummy stroked her hair and hummed the rain song. "I'm here, chinni." Usha curled up smaller. When Dr Lokesh called her name, Mummy carried her in, even though Usha was a big girl now. Afterwards, at home, Mummy sat by her bed and held her hand. "Is it okay that I can't play?" Usha whispered. "It's okay to rest. I love you when you're running, and I love you when you're resting." Usha slept.

qa.q: What song did Mummy hum?
qa.a: Mummy hummed the rain song.

qa.q: What was Usha feeling as she curled up on Mummy's lap?
qa.a: She felt small, tired and heavy, but also warm and safe being held by Mummy.

qa.q: How did Mummy show Usha that resting is okay?
qa.a: She sat by her bed, held her hand and told her she is loved whether she is running or resting.

qa.q: What is it like for Mummy to carry Usha into the doctor's room?
qa.a: Mummy likely feels worried and tender, wanting to keep her daughter close while she is unwell.

grounding: A young girl has a fever and her mother holds her and sits by her bed, so she feels small, warm and safe.

passage:
Monday: Jasleen's forehead was burning. She couldn't finish her roti. Mummy wrapped her in a shawl and held her on the bed all evening, singing softly.
Tuesday: Jasleen stayed home. Mummy sat on the edge of the bed, sewing. Every time Jasleen woke, Mummy was there. Her brother Tanvir peeped in with a paper boat. "For you, sick girl."
Thursday: Jasleen sat up and ate khichdi. "Mummy, I was very lazy." Mummy laughed. "You were resting. Being sick is not lazy."

qa.q: What did Tanvir bring Jasleen on Tuesday?
qa.a: He brought her a paper boat.

qa.q: How did Jasleen feel on Tuesday each time she woke?
qa.a: She felt safe and cared for, because every time she woke, Mummy was there.

qa.q: What did Mummy teach Jasleen on Thursday?
qa.a: That resting when sick is not lazy; it is okay to be weak and still loved.

qa.q: How might Tanvir see his sister being sick?
qa.a: He may feel a little worried and caring, so he makes her a paper boat to cheer her up. 🤍

grounding: Over a few days of fever, a young girl's mother holds her and stays by her bed, teaching her that resting is okay.

passage:
From Irawati's baby book, written by her papa, Tenzin.
Today was the vaccination at the clinic. In the queue Irawati said, "Last time Nani said it won't hurt, and it did." She held my shirt so hard her knuckles went white, and cried. Her heart was thumping under my hand. The nurse knelt down and said, "It will pinch for a second, and I am here. Papa is here too." Irawati squeezed my hand. It was over fast. She sniffed and said, "Only a little pinch. She told the truth." She chose a star sticker.

qa.q: What sticker did Irawati choose?
qa.a: She chose a star sticker.

qa.q: How was Irawati feeling in the queue?
qa.a: She was frightened, holding Papa's shirt tight and crying, with her heart thumping, because last time she had been told it wouldn't hurt.

qa.q: Why did the nurse's words help more than Nani's did last time?
qa.a: The nurse told the truth that it would pinch for a second and stayed with her, so Irawati could trust her.

qa.q: How might Tenzin feel with Irawati's heart thumping under his hand?
qa.a: He probably feels tender and a little anxious for her, wanting to keep her calm and safe.

grounding: A young girl is scared of a vaccination needle, and a nurse honestly says it will pinch for a second while staying with her.

passage: At the health centre in the village, Gautam hid behind his mother's sari when he saw the needle. "No! No!" he cried. His heart was thumping like a drum. His mother, Nandini, knelt. "It will pinch, beta. Just for a second. I am right here." "Will it hurt?" "A little pinch. Then it's finished." The nurse didi held up a toy parrot for him to look at. Gautam held Nandini's hand, squeezed his eyes shut and felt a sharp pinch. "Oh," he said, surprised. "That was all?" He wiped his tears and asked to hold the parrot.

qa.q: What did the nurse didi hold up for Gautam?
qa.a: She held up a toy parrot for him to look at.

qa.q: How was Gautam feeling when he saw the needle?
qa.a: He felt very scared, hiding behind his mother's sari with his heart thumping like a drum.

qa.q: Why was it wise for Nandini to say it would pinch?
qa.a: Telling the truth kept his trust, so the next visit won't feel like a trick.

qa.q: How might Nandini feel when Gautam says "That was all?"
qa.a: She likely feels relieved and proud of him for being brave. 😊

grounding: A young boy is scared of the needle, and his mother tells him the truth that it will pinch for a second and stays with him.
